Whatever the merits of the disagreement between Justices Gorsuch and 
Barrett (which are difficult to evaluate because the two seem to be tallying past 
each other regarding a voluminous and complex record), the Justices in the 
majority seem to be operating in the same tradition of arbitrary-or-capricious 
review as their predecessors in State Farm. And the dissenting Justices may 
generally identify with that tradition, as well, notwithstanding their 
disagreement about its application in this one case. Two of the dissenters, 
Justices Sotomayor and Kagan, joined Justice Breyer’s partial concurrence in 
Department of Commerce v. New York, 588 U.S. 752, 801-21 (2019), which took 
a similarly searching approach to arbitrary-or-capricious review.
3. THE PROCEDURAL REQUIREMENTS 
OF APA SECTION 553
a. Exceptions to the Notice and Comment, Requirements of 
Section 553
So far, this chapter has focused mainly on rules that are required to 
be promulgated through the notice-and-comment procedures of APA 
section 553, like the ones in Auto. Parts, Nafl Tire, and State Farm. In this 
section, we focus on rules that are not required to be promulgated through 
section 553 s notice-and-comment procedures. Because those procedures 
are extremely burdensome, these excepted rules are, relatively spAaking^ 
quite easy for the agency to issue. Hence, whether a rule must be 
promulgated via notice-and-comment procedures is a high-stakes question.
To discern which rules are subject to notice and comment, we must 
begin with the threshold question of what is a “rule.” APA section 551(4) 
defines “rule” as “the whole or a part of an agency statement of general or 
particular applicability and future effect designed to implement, intATprAt, 
or prescribe law or policy or describing the organization, procedure, or 
practice requirements of an agency * * According to Kristin Hickman 
and Richard Pierce, the “definition suffers from two major problems”: (1) 
“if read literally, [it] is broad enough to encompass virtually any statement 
an agency might make in any context,” and (2) “the explicit inclusion of 
statements ‘of particular applicability’ ” is “confusing,” because “[mjost 
people think of a rule as applying broadly to a generic class of individuals.”
